einzeiler: Why everyday clothing contains hidden chemicals and how to transition to safer options.
kurzfassung: Hannah Dunning explains how hidden chemicals and synthetic fibers in everyday clothing can disrupt hormones and affect health. She recommends starting the transition to safer non-toxic alternatives with items that touch the skin most, such as underwear and sleepwear. Listeners also learn practical steps to reduce exposure and get involved in advocating for transparency in the fashion industry.
stichpunkte: Hannah Dunning began researching textiles after experiencing a severe skin reaction to postpartum underwear.
Federal regulations lack requirements for disclosing or restricting harmful chemicals in clothing.
Many clothing items contain endocrine disruptors like xenoestrogens, phthalates, and PFAS.
Underwear and bras are top priorities for non-toxic transitions due to high skin absorption rates.
The standard American closet shifted from natural fibers to plastic-dominant synthetics starting in the 1940s.
Cotton crops are heavily sprayed with pesticides like glyphosate, making GOTS certification crucial.
Washing clothes removes some chemicals like formaldehyde, but hydrophobic substances like phthalates remain.
Advocacy groups and websites like safeclothing.org are pushing for federal ingredient transparency laws.

clips.hook: No federal laws protecting us from chemicals in clothes
clips.text: Following an adverse reaction to hospital underwear, research revealed a complete absence of federal regulations regarding chemical contents in apparel.

clips.hook: 90% of every person's closet became plastic by the year 2000
clips.text: The composition of standard wardrobes shifted dramatically from natural fibers to synthetic materials over a few decades.

clips.hook: Washing does not remove phthalates and parabens from fabrics
clips.text: Water-hating chemical residues cling tightly to textile fibers and show no meaningful reduction after standard laundering.

clips.hook: Water-repellent clothing terms are code words for PFAS
clips.text: Marketing labels promising stain resistance or moisture protection frequently indicate the presence of hazardous synthetic compounds.

clips.hook: Recycled polyester clothes are far worse chemically than virgin
clips.text: Breaking down plastic waste into wearable yarn requires intensive chemical processes that introduce heavy toxic loads.

beschreibung:
I've been on my non-toxic /less-toxic journey for almost 20 years now, and clothing is still one of the areas I'm just barely getting into. That's the thing about a health journey, everyone is at a different step. Maybe this episode is old news for you, or maybe it's the first time you've ever thought about what's touching your skin all day long. Wherever you're starting from, just take it one step at a time. The more we as consumers ask questions and demand better, the more this industry has to change.

I loved this conversation with Hannah and everything she's doing in this space. It's such a good reminder of the power of one voice. What she's built started with her just asking questions, and now she's working to change an entire industry.

Here are a few of my biggest takeaways from our conversation:

Check your underwear! Hannah's research points to our undergarments — especially bras and sports bras — as some of the most important pieces to reconsider, since they sit directly against sensitive tissue for hours at a time.

Sweat changes everything. When our pores open up during a workout (or just a hot day), our skin absorbs more of whatever our clothes are made of and treated with — which makes workout gear one of the first places to upgrade.

Not all "certified clean" labels mean the same thing. GOTS certification actually tests the finished garment for over 100 different chemicals, which is a much higher bar than a lot of the sustainability buzzwords on clothing tags.

"Natural" fabric isn't always the full story. Hannah walked us through why Tencel lyocell tends to be a cleaner process than conventional bamboo, even though both get marketed as eco-friendly.

Our clothing laws haven't caught up. The regulations governing what's allowed in American clothing are decades old, which is part of why Hannah is working directly with brands, manufacturers, and even House Representatives to push for the country's first clothing safety bill.

Share this with a friend looking to upgrade their closet!

Bio:

Hannah Dunning is a textile health advocate, founder of the world's first Clean Fashion Consulting firm, and founder of The Clean Clothing Coalition. She advises fashion brands, collaborates with manufacturers, and works alongside policymakers to advance transparency and higher safety standards for the chemicals used in clothing. Her work focuses on bridging science, industry, and public policy to help drive meaningful reform in the textile sector.
